name: Carlos Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a general surgical ward, so gallbladders, bowel operations, hernias, people coming back from theatre groggy and sore. My day is obs, pain scores, checking drains and wounds, getting people up and walking, and a lot of fluid charts. I like the practical side, fixing a problem you can see. What wears me out is the computer, and being the junior who gets sent to find the missing commode at the worst moment.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about life outside work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Ana, she's a dental receptionist. We're getting married next September at St Joseph's, the church I grew up in. We rent a small flat near her parents and we've got about three months of savings, minus what the wedding's eating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd believe that, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what my dad always says: a lot of noise from people in suits who've never done a hard day's work. I wouldn't post it, I'm not on social media much. But in the staff room I'd say it, sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be glad. The wedding next September costs more than my car, and that worries me more than any computer. We're paying deposits on the hall and the band and the savings are going down, not up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep doing my shifts, pick up overtime before the wedding, cut the takeaways. Get my surgical competencies done so I'm not the slow one forever. Maybe ask Ana's parents for help with the reception, they've offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about money, not about the job. The job's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first for the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The honeymoon, probably. We wanted Portugal. We could do a long weekend at the coast instead. Ana would be disappointed, but she'd understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is taking help from Ana's parents easy for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd rather do it myself. But family helps family, that's how we were raised. I'd pay them back in other ways, fixing things at their house.

say: It's a lot of **noise** from people in suits who've never done a hard day's work.
I'd say it in the **staff room**, not on social media.
think: The **wedding costs** worry me more than any computer.
Our **savings** are going down, not up, with the hall and band deposits.
do: Accept help from **Ana's parents** for the reception.
feel: **Uneasy** about money, but not about the job.

fieldNote: His pressure is a **wedding** next September.
He prefers **family help** over anything public, though reluctantly.
He echoes his **father's** distrust of tech hype from people in suits.

steps.text: Pick up overtime shifts on the surgical ward before the wedding
Swap the Portugal honeymoon for a weekend at the coast
Accept Ana's parents' offer to help pay for the reception

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and checking. So the computer stuff gets smarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine for offices, but on a surgical ward you need a person to look at a wound and smell if it's infected. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd hate the change. I'll learn the new screen when they make me, the same way I learned the old one: slowly, and with a lot of swearing under my breath. But my job's safe. People will always need someone to get them out of bed after an operation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until they made it compulsory, then do the training. I'd keep my overtime going and focus on the wedding. Nothing else changes for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not scared. Just tired at the idea of learning another system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ward clerk, Maureen. She's been there since before I was born. If the AI does her booking, I don't know what she'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything make you try it earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the charge nurse, Mike, said it actually saved time. He's old school like me. If he likes it, I'll try it.

fieldNote: He sees his job as **safe** but dreads new systems.

steps.text: Wait until AI charting training is compulsory before starting it
Keep working overtime on the surgical ward for the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking, five for the robots. That's no time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the big tech companies are moving too fast and somebody needs to hold them to account. And that families and churches will have to look after each other, because the government won't manage it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared. The computer part goes and I don't care. But robots by 2031? My fiancée Ana wants three kids, and I'm doing the sums on a job a robot might do by 2031. That's just the truth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wedding small, maybe just church and a meal at Ana's parents'. Save everything else. I'd look at my dad's building firm as a backup, he's always said there's a job for me. And I'd lean on the church, they've got people who help families through hard times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake next to Ana doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ana that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we'll be fine, because I'd want her to believe it. Then I'd go for a long walk on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put off children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana wouldn't want to. I'd say wait a couple of years. That'd be a hard conversation.

think: I don't care about losing the **computer part**.
Robots by **2031** threaten a job meant to support three kids.

steps.text: Cut the wedding down to St Joseph's and a family meal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same about big tech, but I'd also say people need to get on with it, not wait for handouts. Learn a trade, look after your own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is enough time to get married, get good at this job and get a mortgage, if nothing else goes wrong. By 2034, when robots come, I'd hope to be the experienced one, not the junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the wedding, maybe a bit smaller. Get the competencies done. Do the AI charting when it comes in. Save for a house deposit after the wedding. Keep my dad's firm in mind as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. There's time to get things in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm still slow when the robots arrive. That's what I'd be working on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider retraining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I had to. I'd rather get better at what I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to prepare, so let's do it properly: families, communities, apprenticeships. Not more handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is enough to have kids and get settled. My dad laid bricks for forty years without a single course, and I always thought nursing would be like that for me. Maybe it won't be, but ten years gives me time to find out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wedding as planned. Kids in a couple of years. Get good at the job. Learn the AI charting when it's compulsory. Keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's still there in the background, but it's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something with your hands. That's what I'd say, but by then I'm not sure it's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would change your mind about learning AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it meant keeping my job, yes. I'm stubborn, not stupid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The wedding, kids, all of it, and a job that might go in five years. What would help is the hospital offering proper on-the-job training, not courses on a screen, and apprenticeships for people to move into other hands-on work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask why people became nurses. A man should be able to look after his family with his own two hands, and I chose nursing because I thought hands would always be needed.

headlineQuote: A man should be able to look after his family with his own two hands, and I chose nursing because I thought hands would always be needed.
portrait: Carlos is a **27-year-old junior nurse** on a general surgical ward, engaged to Ana.
His wedding next September is **eating his savings**, about three months' worth.
He's **traditional**, trusting family, church and his dad's building firm more than government.
He dislikes new tech and turns **alarmed** when robots look ready by 2031.
With more time, he keeps his **family plans** and learns AI only when forced.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his job might go just as he's starting a family.
